findings.summary: A changed file is outside the expected deliverables list and was not planned.
findings.evidence: The diff changes an_unplanned_jobs_status_text_and_json_gain_nothing. The old assertion was that the status text never contains 'plan'; the new throughput section's 'planning' stage label broke it. The test now removes the throughput section before checking for 'plan', so its intent is kept. store.rs and display.rs are also off the deliverables list, but they were planned and needed.

findings.summary: Waits between stages inside a job are not measured, and the same waits count as working time when idle time is worked out.
findings.evidence: A job's minutes are the sum of its stage minutes. Wall-clock time between invocations, such as between `athena ask` reading a request and the work starting, falls in no stage. working_span runs from the first invocation to the closing record, so the same time also counts as busy in the idle merge. The review's input can therefore miss the waits it is meant to find. A simpler, more correct approach is to report wall-clock minutes per job and an unattributed 'waiting' figure (span minus the stage sum). The design doc does state the current definitions.

findings.summary: The status test is weaker than the planned demonstration.
findings.evidence: There is no job stopped in planning, though the plan promised one, so the not-landed path for such jobs is untested. Only job B has planner time, so the planning median is 0 and the producer median stays 15 even if planner minutes were counted as producer: that mistake would pass the test. The worsened trigger is tested only through the pure throughput_due function, not through Athena::throughput_review.

findings.summary: A follow-up can be measured from a single landed job.
findings.evidence: FOLLOWUP_MIN_JOBS = 1. The prediction is closed once, so a noisy median from one job becomes the permanent predicted-versus-measured result. Waiting for a few more landings (for example 3 to 5) would give a steadier result.

summary: The change does what was asked. `athena status` gets a throughput section built from job records: landed jobs per UTC day, the median minutes per landed job with a median for each of the six stages, idle time between jobs, and minutes spent on jobs that did not land. A throughput review runs from the drain-start and sweep passes. It is due every 10 landings (`code_health::REVIEW_EVERY`), or when the median is more than 20% worse than at the previous review, once a job has landed since. It asks the verifier's model (a fake model in tests), queues one design request through `StewardRequest` and sets its priority from the predicted minutes saved (2 normal, 5 high, 10 urgent). While that request is open, later reviews queue nothing and do not ask the model. The prediction is kept in a new `athena.throughput-review/1` record. A later review compares the predicted saving with the minutes it measured after a landed change that cites the review. I ran `cargo test -p athena-core status` (25 passed), `cargo test -p athena-core hestia` (24 passed) and `cargo test -p athena-data records` (52 passed). The new tests assert exact numbers. The recorded fmt, clippy and full test runs passed. The CHANGELOG entry and design-doc section 12 state the cadence and the follow-up. Minor findings: (1) `crates/athena-cli/tests/job_plan.rs` changed although it is not on the deliverables list; (2) waits between stages inside a job count in no stage, and the same waits count as working time when idle time is worked out; (3) the status test lacks the planned job stopped in planning and cannot catch planner minutes counted as producer; (4) a follow-up can be measured from a single landed job.
